method: A link over flat ground sees two rays: the direct path between the antennas and the path that reflects off the ground. Their length difference grows with the span, so beyond a breakpoint the two rays arrive almost out of phase and their sum falls away faster than in free space. The wavelength is lambda = c / f with c = 299792458 metres per second. The breakpoint distance, where both models cross, is d_bp = 4 * pi * h_t * h_r / lambda with both antenna heights and the result in the same unit. Inside the breakpoint the tool uses the free-space law L = 20 * log10(4 * pi * d / lambda); past it, the plane-earth law L = 40 * log10(d) - 20 * log10(h_t) - 20 * log10(h_r), with the span and heights in metres. Both branches give exactly the same loss at the breakpoint, and ten times the distance adds 40 dB past it instead of 20 dB inside it. The received power is P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r - L, because the quoted path loss is between isotropic antennas and each antenna gain is counted once. The extra loss from the ground is the path loss minus the free-space loss, floored at zero. One foot is exactly 0.3048 metres, and every length can be entered in metres or feet; the frequency runs from 1 to 10000 MHz, the span from 1 to 50000 metres, each antenna height from 0.1 to 500 metres, the transmit power from 0 to 100 dBm and each antenna gain from 0 to 60 dBi. Inputs accept at most four decimals and no sign or exponent notation; blank, malformed and out-of-range values are refused with a field-specific message. Results are rounded half away from zero to two decimals for losses, powers and lengths, and four for the wavelength. A span shorter than the two heights added together, an antenna below one wavelength, or more than 40 dB of extra ground loss each raise a note rather than an error. The model assumes smooth flat ground, no obstruction, both antennas well above the ground in the far field and a total reflection; terrain, buildings, vegetation and the curved earth all change the answer, so treat it as a planning estimate. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Standard treatments of the two-ray ground reflection (plane-earth) model, such as Rappaport, Wireless Communications: Principles and Practice, which gives the breakpoint distance 4*pi*h_t*h_r/lambda and the 40 dB per decade loss law beyond it.
Radio planning practice for VHF and UHF links: the flat-ground two-ray result is a best-case estimate used where the ground is smooth and no obstruction, curvature or vegetation intervenes.
NIST / ISO 31-1 constants: the speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299792458 m/s and one foot is exactly 0.3048 m.
